speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Did you hear what I was playing, Lane?

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: I didn’t think it polite to listen, sir.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I’m sorry for that, for your sake. I don’t play accurately—any one can play accurately—but I play with wonderful expression. As far as the piano is concerned, sentiment is my forte. I keep science for Life.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Yes, sir.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: And, speaking of the science of Life, have you got the cucumber sandwiches cut for Lady Bracknell?

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Yes, sir.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh! . . . by the way, Lane, I see from your book that on Thursday night, when Lord Shoreman and Mr. Worthing were dining with me, eight bottles of champagne are entered as having been consumed.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Yes, sir; eight bottles and a pint.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Why is it that at a bachelor’s establishment the servants invariably drink the champagne? I ask merely for information.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: I attribute it to the superior quality of the wine, sir. I have often observed that in married households the champagne is rarely of a first-rate brand.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Good heavens! Is marriage so demoralising as that?

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: I believe it is a very pleasant state, sir. I have had very little experience of it myself up to the present. I have only been married once. That was in consequence of a misunderstanding between myself and a young person.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I don’t know that I am much interested in your family life, Lane.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: No, sir; it is not a very interesting subject. I never think of it myself.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Very natural, I am sure. That will do, Lane, thank you.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Thank you, sir.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Lane’s views on marriage seem somewhat lax. Really, if the lower orders don’t set us a good example, what on earth is the use of them? They seem, as a class, to have absolutely no sense of moral responsibility.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Mr. Ernest Worthing.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: How are you, my dear Ernest? What brings you up to town?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, pleasure, pleasure! What else should bring one anywhere? Eating as usual, I see, Algy!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I believe it is customary in good society to take some slight refreshment at five o’clock. Where have you been since last Thursday?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: In the country.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: What on earth do you do there?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: When one is in town one amuses oneself. When one is in the country one amuses other people. It is excessively boring.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: And who are the people you amuse?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, neighbours, neighbours.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Got nice neighbours in your part of Shropshire?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Perfectly horrid! Never speak to one of them.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: How immensely you must amuse them! By the way, Shropshire is your county, is it not?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Eh? Shropshire? Yes, of course. Hallo! Why all these cups? Why cucumber sandwiches? Why such reckless extravagance in one so young? Who is coming to tea?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh! merely Aunt Augusta and Gwendolen.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: How perfectly delightful!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes, that is all very well; but I am afraid Aunt Augusta won’t quite approve of your being here.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: May I ask why?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: My dear fellow, the way you flirt with Gwendolen is perfectly disgraceful. It is almost as bad as the way Gwendolen flirts with you.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I am in love with Gwendolen. I have come up to town expressly to propose to her.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I thought you had come up for pleasure? . . . I call that business.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: How utterly unromantic you are!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I really don’t see anything romantic in proposing. It is very romantic to be in love. But there is nothing romantic about a definite proposal. Why, one may be accepted. One usually is, I believe. Then the excitement is all over. The very essence of romance is uncertainty. If ever I get married, I’ll certainly try to forget the fact.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I have no doubt about that, dear Algy. The Divorce Court was specially invented for people whose memories are so curiously constituted.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh! there is no use speculating on that subject. Divorces are made in Heaven— Please don’t touch the cucumber sandwiches. They are ordered specially for Aunt Augusta.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, you have been eating them all the time.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: That is quite a different matter. She is my aunt. Have some bread and butter. The bread and butter is for Gwendolen. Gwendolen is devoted to bread and butter.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: And very good bread and butter it is too.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, my dear fellow, you need not eat as if you were going to eat it all. You behave as if you were married to her already. You are not married to her already, and I don’t think you ever will be.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Why on earth do you say that?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, in the first place girls never marry the men they flirt with. Girls don’t think it right.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, that is nonsense!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: It isn’t. It is a great truth. It accounts for the extraordinary number of bachelors that one sees all over the place. In the second place, I don’t give my consent.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Your consent!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: My dear fellow, Gwendolen is my first cousin. And before I allow you to marry her, you will have to clear up the whole question of Cecily.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Cecily! What on earth do you mean? What do you mean, Algy, by Cecily! I don’t know any one of the name of Cecily.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Bring me that cigarette case Mr. Worthing left in the smoking-room the last time he dined here.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Yes, sir.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Do you mean to say you have had my cigarette case all this time? I wish to goodness you had let me know. I have been writing frantic letters to Scotland Yard about it. I was very nearly offering a large reward.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, I wish you would offer one. I happen to be more than usually hard up.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: There is no good offering a large reward now that the thing is found.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I think that is rather mean of you, Ernest, I must say. However, it makes no matter, for, now that I look at the inscription inside, I find that the thing isn’t yours after all.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Of course it’s mine. You have seen me with it a hundred times, and you have no right whatsoever to read what is written inside. It is a very ungentlemanly thing to read a private cigarette case.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh! it is absurd to have a hard and fast rule about what one should read and what one shouldn’t. More than half of modern culture depends on what one shouldn’t read.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I am quite aware of the fact, and I don’t propose to discuss modern culture. It isn’t the sort of thing one should talk of in private. I simply want my cigarette case back.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes; but this isn’t your cigarette case. This cigarette case is a present from some one of the name of Cecily, and you said you didn’t know any one of that name.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, if you want to know, Cecily happens to be my aunt.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Your aunt!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Yes. Charming old lady she is, too. Lives at Tunbridge Wells. Just give it back to me, Algy.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: But why does she call herself little Cecily if she is your aunt and lives at Tunbridge Wells? ‘From little Cecily with her fondest love.’

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: My dear fellow, what on earth is there in that? Some aunts are tall, some aunts are not tall. That is a matter that surely an aunt may be allowed to decide for herself. You seem to think that every aunt should be exactly like your aunt! That is absurd! For Heaven’s sake give me back my cigarette case.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes. But why does your aunt call you her uncle? ‘From little Cecily, with her fondest love to her dear Uncle Jack.’ There is no objection, I admit, to an aunt being a small aunt, but why an aunt, no matter what her size may be, should call her own nephew her uncle, I can’t quite make out. Besides, your name isn’t Jack at all; it is Ernest.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: It isn’t Ernest; it’s Jack.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: You have always told me it was Ernest. I have introduced you to every one as Ernest. You answer to the name of Ernest. You look as if your name was Ernest. You are the most earnest-looking person I ever saw in my life. It is perfectly absurd your saying that your name isn’t Ernest. It’s on your cards. Here is one of them. ‘Mr. Ernest Worthing, B. 4, The Albany.’ I’ll keep this as a proof that your name is Ernest if ever you attempt to deny it to me, or to Gwendolen, or to any one else.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, my name is Ernest in town and Jack in the country, and the cigarette case was given to me in the country.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes, but that does not account for the fact that your small Aunt Cecily, who lives at Tunbridge Wells, calls you her dear uncle. Come, old boy, you had much better have the thing out at once.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: My dear Algy, you talk exactly as if you were a dentist. It is very vulgar to talk like a dentist when one isn’t a dentist. It produces a false impression.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, that is exactly what dentists always do. Now, go on! Tell me the whole thing. I may mention that I have always suspected you of being a confirmed and secret Bunburyist; and I am quite sure of it now.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Bunburyist? What on earth do you mean by a Bunburyist?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I’ll reveal to you the meaning of that incomparable expression as soon as you are kind enough to inform me why you are Ernest in town and Jack in the country.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, produce my cigarette case first.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Here it is. Now produce your explanation, and pray make it improbable.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: My dear fellow, there is nothing improbable about my explanation at all. In fact it’s perfectly ordinary. Old Mr. Thomas Cardew, who adopted me when I was a little boy, made me in his will guardian to his grand-daughter, Miss Cecily Cardew. Cecily, who addresses me as her uncle from motives of respect that you could not possibly appreciate, lives at my place in the country under the charge of her admirable governess, Miss Prism.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Where is that place in the country, by the way?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: That is nothing to you, dear boy. You are not going to be invited . . . I may tell you candidly that the place is not in Shropshire.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I suspected that, my dear fellow! I have Bunburyed all over Shropshire on two separate occasions. Now, go on. Why are you Ernest in town and Jack in the country?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: My dear Algy, I don’t know whether you will be able to understand my real motives. You are hardly serious enough. When one is placed in the position of guardian, one has to adopt a very high moral tone on all subjects. It’s one’s duty to do so. And as a high moral tone can hardly be said to conduce very much to either one’s health or one’s happiness, in order to get up to town I have always pretended to have a younger brother of the name of Ernest, who lives in the Albany, and gets into the most dreadful scrapes. That, my dear Algy, is the whole truth pure and simple.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: The truth is rarely pure and never simple. Modern life would be very tedious if it were either, and modern literature a complete impossibility!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: That wouldn’t be at all a bad thing.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Literary criticism is not your forte, my dear fellow. Don’t try it. You should leave that to people who haven’t been at a University. They do it so well in the daily papers. What you really are is a Bunburyist. I was quite right in saying you were a Bunburyist. You are one of the most advanced Bunburyists I know.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: What on earth do you mean?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: You have invented a very useful younger brother called Ernest, in order that you may be able to come up to town as often as you like. I have invented an invaluable permanent invalid called Bunbury, in order that I may be able to go down into the country whenever I choose. Bunbury is perfectly invaluable. If it wasn’t for Bunbury’s extraordinary bad health, for instance, I wouldn’t be able to dine with you at Willis’s to-night, for I have been really engaged to Aunt Augusta for more than a week.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I haven’t asked you to dine with me anywhere to-night.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I know. You are absurdly careless about sending out invitations. It is very foolish of you. Nothing annoys people so much as not receiving invitations.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: You had much better dine with your Aunt Augusta.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I haven’t the smallest intention of doing anything of the kind. To begin with, I dined there on Monday, and once a week is quite enough to dine with one’s own relations. In the second place, whenever I do dine there I am always treated as a member of the family, and sent down with either no woman at all, or two. In the third place, I know perfectly well whom she will place me next to, to-night. She will place me next Mary Farquhar, who always flirts with her own husband across the dinner-table. That is not very pleasant. Indeed, it is not even decent . . . and that sort of thing is enormously on the increase. The amount of women in London who flirt with their own husbands is perfectly scandalous. It looks so bad. It is simply washing one’s clean linen in public. Besides, now that I know you to be a confirmed Bunburyist I naturally want to talk to you about Bunburying. I want to tell you the rules.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I’m not a Bunburyist at all. If Gwendolen accepts me, I am going to kill my brother, indeed I think I’ll kill him in any case. Cecily is a little too much interested in him. It is rather a bore. So I am going to get rid of Ernest. And I strongly advise you to do the same with Mr. . . . with your invalid friend who has the absurd name.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Nothing will induce me to part with Bunbury, and if you ever get married, which seems to me extremely problematic, you will be very glad to know Bunbury. A man who marries without knowing Bunbury has a very tedious time of it.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: That is nonsense. If I marry a charming girl like Gwendolen, and she is the only girl I ever saw in my life that I would marry, I certainly won’t want to know Bunbury.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Then your wife will. You don’t seem to realise, that in married life three is company and two is none.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: That, my dear young friend, is the theory that the corrupt French Drama has been propounding for the last fifty years.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes; and that the happy English home has proved in half the time.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: For heaven’s sake, don’t try to be cynical. It’s perfectly easy to be cynical.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: My dear fellow, it isn’t easy to be anything nowadays. There’s such a lot of beastly competition about. Ah! that must be Aunt Augusta. Only relatives, or creditors, ever ring in that Wagnerian manner. Now, if I get her out of the way for ten minutes, so that you can have an opportunity for proposing to Gwendolen, may I dine with you to-night at Willis’s?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I suppose so, if you want to.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes, but you must be serious about it. I hate people who are not serious about meals. It is so shallow of them.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Lady Bracknell and Miss Fairfax.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Good afternoon, dear Algernon, I hope you are behaving very well.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I’m feeling very well, Aunt Augusta.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: That’s not quite the same thing. In fact the two things rarely go together.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Dear me, you are smart!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I am always smart! Am I not, Mr. Worthing?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: You’re quite perfect, Miss Fairfax.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Oh! I hope I am not that. It would leave no room for developments, and I intend to develop in many directions.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I’m sorry if we are a little late, Algernon, but I was obliged to call on dear Lady Harbury. I hadn’t been there since her poor husband’s death. I never saw a woman so altered; she looks quite twenty years younger. And now I’ll have a cup of tea, and one of those nice cucumber sandwiches you promised me.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Certainly, Aunt Augusta.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Won’t you come and sit here, Gwendolen?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Thanks, mamma, I’m quite comfortable where I am.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Good heavens! Lane! Why are there no cucumber sandwiches? I ordered them specially.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: There were no cucumbers in the market this morning, sir. I went down twice.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: No cucumbers!

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: No, sir. Not even for ready money.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: That will do, Lane, thank you.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Thank you, sir.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I am greatly distressed, Aunt Augusta, about there being no cucumbers, not even for ready money.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: It really makes no matter, Algernon. I had some crumpets with Lady Harbury, who seems to me to be living entirely for pleasure now.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I hear her hair has turned quite gold from grief.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: It certainly has changed its colour. From what cause I, of course, cannot say. Thank you. I’ve quite a treat for you to-night, Algernon. I am going to send you down with Mary Farquhar. She is such a nice woman, and so attentive to her husband. It’s delightful to watch them.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I am afraid, Aunt Augusta, I shall have to give up the pleasure of dining with you to-night after all.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I hope not, Algernon. It would put my table completely out. Your uncle would have to dine upstairs. Fortunately he is accustomed to that.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: It is a great bore, and, I need hardly say, a terrible disappointment to me, but the fact is I have just had a telegram to say that my poor friend Bunbury is very ill again. They seem to think I should be with him.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: It is very strange. This Mr. Bunbury seems to suffer from curiously bad health.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes; poor Bunbury is a dreadful invalid.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Well, I must say, Algernon, that I think it is high time that Mr. Bunbury made up his mind whether he was going to live or to die. This shilly-shallying with the question is absurd. Nor do I in any way approve of the modern sympathy with invalids. I consider it morbid. Illness of any kind is hardly a thing to be encouraged in others. Health is the primary duty of life. I am always telling that to your poor uncle, but he never seems to take much notice . . . as far as any improvement in his ailment goes. I should be much obliged if you would ask Mr. Bunbury, from me, to be kind enough not to have a relapse on Saturday, for I rely on you to arrange my music for me. It is my last reception, and one wants something that will encourage conversation, particularly at the end of the season when every one has practically said whatever they had to say, which, in most cases, was probably not much.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I’ll speak to Bunbury, Aunt Augusta, if he is still conscious, and I think I can promise you he’ll be all right by Saturday. Of course the music is a great difficulty. You see, if one plays good music, people don’t listen, and if one plays bad music people don’t talk. But I’ll run over the programme I’ve drawn out, if you will kindly come into the next room for a moment.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Thank you, Algernon. It is very thoughtful of you. I’m sure the programme will be delightful, after a few expurgations. French songs I cannot possibly allow. People always seem to think that they are improper, and either look shocked, which is vulgar, or laugh, which is worse. But German sounds a thoroughly respectable language, and indeed, I believe is so. Gwendolen, you will accompany me.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Certainly, mamma.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Charming day it has been, Miss Fairfax.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Pray don’t talk to me about the weather, Mr. Worthing. Whenever people talk to me about the weather, I always feel quite certain that they mean something else. And that makes me so nervous.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I do mean something else.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I thought so. In fact, I am never wrong.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: And I would like to be allowed to take advantage of Lady Bracknell’s temporary absence . . .

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I would certainly advise you to do so. Mamma has a way of coming back suddenly into a room that I have often had to speak to her about.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Miss Fairfax, ever since I met you I have admired you more than any girl . . . I have ever met since . . . I met you.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Yes, I am quite well aware of the fact. And I often wish that in public, at any rate, you had been more demonstrative. For me you have always had an irresistible fascination. Even before I met you I was far from indifferent to you. We live, as I hope you know, Mr. Worthing, in an age of ideals. The fact is constantly mentioned in the more expensive monthly magazines, and has reached the provincial pulpits, I am told; and my ideal has always been to love some one of the name of Ernest. There is something in that name that inspires absolute confidence. The moment Algernon first mentioned to me that he had a friend called Ernest, I knew I was destined to love you.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: You really love me, Gwendolen?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Passionately!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Darling! You don’t know how happy you’ve made me.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: My own Ernest!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: But you don’t really mean to say that you couldn’t love me if my name wasn’t Ernest?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: But your name is Ernest.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Yes, I know it is. But supposing it was something else? Do you mean to say you couldn’t love me then?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Ah! that is clearly a metaphysical speculation, and like most metaphysical speculations has very little reference at all to the actual facts of real life, as we know them.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Personally, darling, to speak quite candidly, I don’t much care about the name of Ernest . . . I don’t think the name suits me at all.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: It suits you perfectly. It is a divine name. It has a music of its own. It produces vibrations.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, really, Gwendolen, I must say that I think there are lots of other much nicer names. I think Jack, for instance, a charming name.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Jack? . . . No, there is very little music in the name Jack, if any at all, indeed. It does not thrill. It produces absolutely no vibrations . . . I have known several Jacks, and they all, without exception, were more than usually plain. Besides, Jack is a notorious domesticity for John! And I pity any woman who is married to a man called John. She would probably never be allowed to know the entrancing pleasure of a single moment’s solitude. The only really safe name is Ernest.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Gwendolen, I must get christened at once—I mean we must get married at once. There is no time to be lost.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Married, Mr. Worthing?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well . . . surely. You know that I love you, and you led me to believe, Miss Fairfax, that you were not absolutely indifferent to me.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I adore you. But you haven’t proposed to me yet. Nothing has been said at all about marriage. The subject has not even been touched on.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well . . . may I propose to you now?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I think it would be an admirable opportunity. And to spare you any possible disappointment, Mr. Worthing, I think it only fair to tell you quite frankly before-hand that I am fully determined to accept you.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Gwendolen!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Yes, Mr. Worthing, what have you got to say to me?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: You know what I have got to say to you.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Yes, but you don’t say it.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Gwendolen, will you marry me?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Of course I will, darling. How long you have been about it! I am afraid you have had very little experience in how to propose.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: My own one, I have never loved any one in the world but you.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Yes, but men often propose for practice. I know my brother Gerald does. All my girl-friends tell me so. What wonderfully blue eyes you have, Ernest! They are quite, quite, blue. I hope you will always look at me just like that, especially when there are other people present.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Mr. Worthing! Rise, sir, from this semi-recumbent posture. It is most indecorous.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Mamma! I must beg you to retire. This is no place for you. Besides, Mr. Worthing has not quite finished yet.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Finished what, may I ask?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Mamma!

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen! Gwendolen, the carriage!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Yes, mamma.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Twenty-nine.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: In land, or in investments?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: In investments, chiefly.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: The unfashionable side. I thought there was something. However, that could easily be altered.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Do you mean the fashion, or the side?

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Both, if necessary, I presume. What are your politics?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, I am afraid I really have none. I am a Liberal Unionist.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Oh, they count as Tories. They dine with us. Or come in the evening, at any rate. Now to minor matters. Are your parents living?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I have lost both my parents.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: To lose one parent, Mr. Worthing, may be regarded as a misfortune; to lose both looks like carelessness. Who was your father? He was evidently a man of some wealth. Was he born in what the Radical papers call the purple of commerce, or did he rise from the ranks of the aristocracy?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I am afraid I really don’t know. The fact is, Lady Bracknell, I said I had lost my parents. It would be nearer the truth to say that my parents seem to have lost me . . . I don’t actually know who I am by birth. I was . . . well, I was found.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Found!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: The late Mr. Thomas Cardew, an old gentleman of a very charitable and kindly disposition, found me, and gave me the name of Worthing, because he happened to have a first-class ticket for Worthing in his pocket at the time. Worthing is a place in Sussex. It is a seaside resort.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Where did the charitable gentleman who had a first-class ticket for this seaside resort find you?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: In a hand-bag.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: A hand-bag?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Yes, Lady Bracknell. I was in a hand-bag—a somewhat large, black leather hand-bag, with handles to it—an ordinary hand-bag in fact.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: In what locality did this Mr. James, or Thomas, Cardew come across this ordinary hand-bag?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: In the cloak-room at Victoria Station. It was given to him in mistake for his own.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: The cloak-room at Victoria Station?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Yes. The Brighton line.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: The line is immaterial. Mr. Worthing, I confess I feel somewhat bewildered by what you have just told me. To be born, or at any rate bred, in a hand-bag, whether it had handles or not, seems to me to display a contempt for the ordinary decencies of family life that reminds one of the worst excesses of the French Revolution. And I presume you know what that unfortunate movement led to? As for the particular locality in which the hand-bag was found, a cloak-room at a railway station might serve to conceal a social indiscretion—has probably, indeed, been used for that purpose before now—but it could hardly be regarded as an assured basis for a recognised position in good society.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: May I ask you then what you would advise me to do? I need hardly say I would do anything in the world to ensure Gwendolen’s happiness.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I would strongly advise you, Mr. Worthing, to try and acquire some relations as soon as possible, and to make a definite effort to produce at any rate one parent, of either sex, before the season is quite over.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, I don’t see how I could possibly manage to do that. I can produce the hand-bag at any moment. It is in my dressing-room at home. I really think that should satisfy you, Lady Bracknell.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Me, sir! What has it to do with me? You can hardly imagine that I and Lord Bracknell would dream of allowing our only daughter—a girl brought up with the utmost care—to marry into a cloak-room, and form an alliance with a parcel? Good morning, Mr. Worthing!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Good morning! For goodness’ sake don’t play that ghastly tune, Algy. How idiotic you are!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Didn’t it go off all right, old boy? You don’t mean to say Gwendolen refused you? I know it is a way she has. She is always refusing people. I think it is most ill-natured of her.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, Gwendolen is as right as a trivet. As far as she is concerned, we are engaged. Her mother is perfectly unbearable. Never met such a Gorgon . . . I don’t really know what a Gorgon is like, but I am quite sure that Lady Bracknell is one. In any case, she is a monster, without being a myth, which is rather unfair . . . I beg your pardon, Algy, I suppose I shouldn’t talk about your own aunt in that way before you.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: My dear boy, I love hearing my relations abused. It is the only thing that makes me put up with them at all. Relations are simply a tedious pack of people, who haven’t got the remotest knowledge of how to live, nor the smallest instinct about when to die.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, that is nonsense!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: It isn’t!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, I won’t argue about the matter. You always want to argue about things.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: That is exactly what things were originally made for.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Upon my word, if I thought that, I’d shoot myself . . . You don’t think there is any chance of Gwendolen becoming like her mother in about a hundred and fifty years, do you, Algy?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: All women become like their mothers. That is their tragedy. No man does. That’s his.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Is that clever?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: It is perfectly phrased! and quite as true as any observation in civilised life should be.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I am sick to death of cleverness. Everybody is clever nowadays. You can’t go anywhere without meeting clever people. The thing has become an absolute public nuisance. I wish to goodness we had a few fools left.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: We have.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I should extremely like to meet them. What do they talk about?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: The fools? Oh! about the clever people, of course.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: What fools!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: By the way, did you tell Gwendolen the truth about your being Ernest in town, and Jack in the country?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: My dear fellow, the truth isn’t quite the sort of thing one tells to a nice, sweet, refined girl. What extraordinary ideas you have about the way to behave to a woman!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: The only way to behave to a woman is to make love to her, if she is pretty, and to some one else, if she is plain.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, that is nonsense.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: What about your brother? What about the profligate Ernest?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, before the end of the week I shall have got rid of him. I’ll say he died in Paris of apoplexy. Lots of people die of apoplexy, quite suddenly, don’t they?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes, but it’s hereditary, my dear fellow. It’s a sort of thing that runs in families. You had much better say a severe chill.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: You are sure a severe chill isn’t hereditary, or anything of that kind?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Of course it isn’t!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Very well, then. My poor brother Ernest is carried off suddenly, in Paris, by a severe chill. That gets rid of him.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: But I thought you said that . . . Miss Cardew was a little too much interested in your poor brother Ernest? Won’t she feel his loss a good deal?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, that is all right. Cecily is not a silly romantic girl, I am glad to say. She has got a capital appetite, goes long walks, and pays no attention at all to her lessons.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I would rather like to see Cecily.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I will take very good care you never do. She is excessively pretty, and she is only just eighteen.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Have you told Gwendolen yet that you have an excessively pretty ward who is only just eighteen?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh! one doesn’t blurt these things out to people. Cecily and Gwendolen are perfectly certain to be extremely great friends. I’ll bet you anything you like that half an hour after they have met, they will be calling each other sister.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Women only do that when they have called each other a lot of other things first. Now, my dear boy, if we want to get a good table at Willis’s, we really must go and dress. Do you know it is nearly seven?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh! It always is nearly seven.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, I’m hungry.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I never knew you when you weren’t . . .

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: What shall we do after dinner? Go to a theatre?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh no! I loathe listening.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, let us go to the Club?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, no! I hate talking.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, we might trot round to the Empire at ten?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, no! I can’t bear looking at things. It is so silly.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, what shall we do?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Nothing!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: It is awfully hard work doing nothing. However, I don’t mind hard work where there is no definite object of any kind.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Miss Fairfax.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Gwendolen, upon my word!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Algy, kindly turn your back. I have something very particular to say to Mr. Worthing.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Really, Gwendolen, I don’t think I can allow this at all.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Algy, you always adopt a strictly immoral attitude towards life. You are not quite old enough to do that.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: My own darling!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Ernest, we may never be married. From the expression on mamma’s face I fear we never shall. Few parents nowadays pay any regard to what their children say to them. The old-fashioned respect for the young is fast dying out. Whatever influence I ever had over mamma, I lost at the age of three. But although she may prevent us from becoming man and wife, and I may marry some one else, and marry often, nothing that she can possibly do can alter my eternal devotion to you.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Dear Gwendolen!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: The story of your romantic origin, as related to me by mamma, with unpleasing comments, has naturally stirred the deeper fibres of my nature. Your Christian name has an irresistible fascination. The simplicity of your character makes you exquisitely incomprehensible to me. Your town address at the Albany I have. What is your address in the country?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: The Manor House, Woolton, Hertfordshire.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: There is a good postal service, I suppose? It may be necessary to do something desperate. That of course will require serious consideration. I will communicate with you daily.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: My own one!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: How long do you remain in town?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Till Monday.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Good! Algy, you may turn round now.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Thanks, I’ve turned round already.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: You may also ring the bell.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: You will let me see you to your carriage, my own darling?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Certainly.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I will see Miss Fairfax out.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Yes, sir.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: A glass of sherry, Lane.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Yes, sir.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: To-morrow, Lane, I’m going Bunburying.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Yes, sir.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I shall probably not be back till Monday. You can put up my dress clothes, my smoking jacket, and all the Bunbury suits . . .

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: Yes, sir.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I hope to-morrow will be a fine day, Lane.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: It never is, sir.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Lane, you’re a perfect pessimist.

speeches.speaker: LANE
speeches.text: I do my best to give satisfaction, sir.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: There’s a sensible, intellectual girl! the only girl I ever cared for in my life. What on earth are you so amused at?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh, I’m a little anxious about poor Bunbury, that is all.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: If you don’t take care, your friend Bunbury will get you into a serious scrape some day.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I love scrapes. They are the only things that are never serious.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, that’s nonsense, Algy. You never talk anything but nonsense.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Nobody ever does.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Cecily, Cecily! Surely such a utilitarian occupation as the watering of flowers is rather Moulton’s duty than yours? Especially at a moment when intellectual pleasures await you. Your German grammar is on the table. Pray open it at page fifteen. We will repeat yesterday’s lesson.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: But I don’t like German. It isn’t at all a becoming language. I know perfectly well that I look quite plain after my German lesson.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Child, you know how anxious your guardian is that you should improve yourself in every way. He laid particular stress on your German, as he was leaving for town yesterday. Indeed, he always lays stress on your German when he is leaving for town.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Dear Uncle Jack is so very serious! Sometimes he is so serious that I think he cannot be quite well.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Your guardian enjoys the best of health, and his gravity of demeanour is especially to be commended in one so comparatively young as he is. I know no one who has a higher sense of duty and responsibility.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I suppose that is why he often looks a little bored when we three are together.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Cecily! I am surprised at you. Mr. Worthing has many troubles in his life. Idle merriment and triviality would be out of place in his conversation. You must remember his constant anxiety about that unfortunate young man his brother.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I wish Uncle Jack would allow that unfortunate young man, his brother, to come down here sometimes. We might have a good influence over him, Miss Prism. I am sure you certainly would. You know German, and geology, and things of that kind influence a man very much.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: I do not think that even I could produce any effect on a character that according to his own brother’s admission is irretrievably weak and vacillating. Indeed I am not sure that I would desire to reclaim him. I am not in favour of this modern mania for turning bad people into good people at a moment’s notice. As a man sows so let him reap. You must put away your diary, Cecily. I really don’t see why you should keep a diary at all.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I keep a diary in order to enter the wonderful secrets of my life. If I didn’t write them down, I should probably forget all about them.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Memory, my dear Cecily, is the diary that we all carry about with us.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Yes, but it usually chronicles the things that have never happened, and couldn’t possibly have happened. I believe that Memory is responsible for nearly all the three-volume novels that Mudie sends us.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Do not speak slightingly of the three-volume novel, Cecily. I wrote one myself in earlier days.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Did you really, Miss Prism? How wonderfully clever you are! I hope it did not end happily? I don’t like novels that end happily. They depress me so much.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: The good ended happily, and the bad unhappily. That is what Fiction means.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I suppose so. But it seems very unfair. And was your novel ever published?

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Alas! no. The manuscript unfortunately was abandoned. I use the word in the sense of lost or mislaid. To your work, child, these speculations are profitless.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: But I see dear Dr. Chasuble coming up through the garden.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Dr. Chasuble! This is indeed a pleasure.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: And how are we this morning? Miss Prism, you are, I trust, well?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Miss Prism has just been complaining of a slight headache. I think it would do her so much good to have a short stroll with you in the Park, Dr. Chasuble.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Cecily, I have not mentioned anything about a headache.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: No, dear Miss Prism, I know that, but I felt instinctively that you had a headache. Indeed I was thinking about that, and not about my German lesson, when the Rector came in.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: I hope, Cecily, you are not inattentive.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh, I am afraid I am.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: That is strange. Were I fortunate enough to be Miss Prism’s pupil, I would hang upon her lips. I spoke metaphorically.—My metaphor was drawn from bees. Ahem! Mr. Worthing, I suppose, has not returned from town yet?

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: We do not expect him till Monday afternoon.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Ah yes, he usually likes to spend his Sunday in London. He is not one of those whose sole aim is enjoyment, as, by all accounts, that unfortunate young man his brother seems to be. But I must not disturb Egeria and her pupil any longer.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Egeria? My name is Lætitia, Doctor.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: A classical allusion merely, drawn from the Pagan authors. I shall see you both no doubt at Evensong?

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: I think, dear Doctor, I will have a stroll with you. I find I have a headache after all, and a walk might do it good.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: With pleasure, Miss Prism, with pleasure. We might go as far as the schools and back.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: That would be delightful. Cecily, you will read your Political Economy in my absence. The chapter on the Fall of the Rupee you may omit. It is somewhat too sensational. Even these metallic problems have their melodramatic side.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Horrid Political Economy! Horrid Geography! Horrid, horrid German!

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Mr. Ernest Worthing has just driven over from the station. He has brought his luggage with him.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: ‘Mr. Ernest Worthing, B. 4, The Albany, W.’ Uncle Jack’s brother! Did you tell him Mr. Worthing was in town?

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Yes, Miss. He seemed very much disappointed. I mentioned that you and Miss Prism were in the garden. He said he was anxious to speak to you privately for a moment.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Ask Mr. Ernest Worthing to come here. I suppose you had better talk to the housekeeper about a room for him.

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Yes, Miss.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I have never met any really wicked person before. I feel rather frightened. I am so afraid he will look just like every one else. He does!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: You are my little cousin Cecily, I’m sure.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: You are under some strange mistake. I am not little. In fact, I believe I am more than usually tall for my age. But I am your cousin Cecily. You, I see from your card, are Uncle Jack’s brother, my cousin Ernest, my wicked cousin Ernest.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh! I am not really wicked at all, cousin Cecily. You mustn’t think that I am wicked.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: If you are not, then you have certainly been deceiving us all in a very inexcusable manner. I hope you have not been leading a double life, pretending to be wicked and being really good all the time. That would be hypocrisy.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh! Of course I have been rather reckless.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I am glad to hear it.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: In fact, now you mention the subject, I have been very bad in my own small way.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I don’t think you should be so proud of that, though I am sure it must have been very pleasant.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: It is much pleasanter being here with you.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I can’t understand how you are here at all. Uncle Jack won’t be back till Monday afternoon.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: That is a great disappointment. I am obliged to go up by the first train on Monday morning. I have a business appointment that I am anxious . . . to miss?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Couldn’t you miss it anywhere but in London?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: No: the appointment is in London.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Well, I know, of course, how important it is not to keep a business engagement, if one wants to retain any sense of the beauty of life, but still I think you had better wait till Uncle Jack arrives. I know he wants to speak to you about your emigrating.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: About my what?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Your emigrating. He has gone up to buy your outfit.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I certainly wouldn’t let Jack buy my outfit. He has no taste in neckties at all.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I don’t think you will require neckties. Uncle Jack is sending you to Australia.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Australia! I’d sooner die.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Well, he said at dinner on Wednesday night, that you would have to choose between this world, the next world, and Australia.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh, well! The accounts I have received of Australia and the next world, are not particularly encouraging. This world is good enough for me, cousin Cecily.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Yes, but are you good enough for it?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I’m afraid I’m not that. That is why I want you to reform me. You might make that your mission, if you don’t mind, cousin Cecily.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I’m afraid I’ve no time, this afternoon.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, would you mind my reforming myself this afternoon?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: It is rather Quixotic of you. But I think you should try.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I will. I feel better already.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: You are looking a little worse.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: That is because I am hungry.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: How thoughtless of me. I should have remembered that when one is going to lead an entirely new life, one requires regular and wholesome meals. Won’t you come in?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Thank you. Might I have a buttonhole first? I never have any appetite unless I have a buttonhole first.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: A Marechal Niel?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: No, I’d sooner have a pink rose.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Why?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Because you are like a pink rose, Cousin Cecily.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I don’t think it can be right for you to talk to me like that. Miss Prism never says such things to me.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Then Miss Prism is a short-sighted old lady. You are the prettiest girl I ever saw.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Miss Prism says that all good looks are a snare.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: They are a snare that every sensible man would like to be caught in.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh, I don’t think I would care to catch a sensible man. I shouldn’t know what to talk to him about.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: You are too much alone, dear Dr. Chasuble. You should get married. A misanthrope I can understand—a womanthrope, never!

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Believe me, I do not deserve so neologistic a phrase. The precept as well as the practice of the Primitive Church was distinctly against matrimony.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: That is obviously the reason why the Primitive Church has not lasted up to the present day. And you do not seem to realise, dear Doctor, that by persistently remaining single, a man converts himself into a permanent public temptation. Men should be more careful; this very celibacy leads weaker vessels astray.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: But is a man not equally attractive when married?

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: No married man is ever attractive except to his wife.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: And often, I’ve been told, not even to her.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: That depends on the intellectual sympathies of the woman. Maturity can always be depended on. Ripeness can be trusted. Young women are green. I spoke horticulturally. My metaphor was drawn from fruits. But where is Cecily?

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Perhaps she followed us to the schools.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Mr. Worthing!

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Mr. Worthing?

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: This is indeed a surprise. We did not look for you till Monday afternoon.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I have returned sooner than I expected. Dr. Chasuble, I hope you are well?

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Dear Mr. Worthing, I trust this garb of woe does not betoken some terrible calamity?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: My brother.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: More shameful debts and extravagance?

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Still leading his life of pleasure?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Dead!

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Your brother Ernest dead?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Quite dead.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: What a lesson for him! I trust he will profit by it.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Mr. Worthing, I offer you my sincere condolence. You have at least the consolation of knowing that you were always the most generous and forgiving of brothers.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Poor Ernest! He had many faults, but it is a sad, sad blow.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Very sad indeed. Were you with him at the end?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: No. He died abroad; in Paris, in fact. I had a telegram last night from the manager of the Grand Hotel.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Was the cause of death mentioned?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: A severe chill, it seems.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: As a man sows, so shall he reap.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Charity, dear Miss Prism, charity! None of us are perfect. I myself am peculiarly susceptible to draughts. Will the interment take place here?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: No. He seems to have expressed a desire to be buried in Paris.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: In Paris! I fear that hardly points to any very serious state of mind at the last. You would no doubt wish me to make some slight allusion to this tragic domestic affliction next Sunday. My sermon on the meaning of the manna in the wilderness can be adapted to almost any occasion, joyful, or, as in the present case, distressing. I have preached it at harvest celebrations, christenings, confirmations, on days of humiliation and festal days. The last time I delivered it was in the Cathedral, as a charity sermon on behalf of the Society for the Prevention of Discontent among the Upper Orders. The Bishop, who was present, was much struck by some of the analogies I drew.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Ah! that reminds me, you mentioned christenings I think, Dr. Chasuble? I suppose you know how to christen all right? I mean, of course, you are continually christening, aren’t you?

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: It is, I regret to say, one of the Rector’s most constant duties in this parish. I have often spoken to the poorer classes on the subject. But they don’t seem to know what thrift is.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: But is there any particular infant in whom you are interested, Mr. Worthing? Your brother was, I believe, unmarried, was he not?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh yes.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: People who live entirely for pleasure usually are.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: But it is not for any child, dear Doctor. I am very fond of children. No! the fact is, I would like to be christened myself, this afternoon, if you have nothing better to do.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: But surely, Mr. Worthing, you have been christened already?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I don’t remember anything about it.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: But have you any grave doubts on the subject?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I certainly intend to have. Of course I don’t know if the thing would bother you in any way, or if you think I am a little too old now.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Not at all. The sprinkling, and, indeed, the immersion of adults is a perfectly canonical practice.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Immersion!

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: You need have no apprehensions. Sprinkling is all that is necessary, or indeed I think advisable. Our weather is so changeable. At what hour would you wish the ceremony performed?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, I might trot round about five if that would suit you.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Perfectly, perfectly! In fact I have two similar ceremonies to perform at that time. A case of twins that occurred recently in one of the outlying cottages on your own estate. Poor Jenkins the carter, a most hard-working man.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh! I don’t see much fun in being christened along with other babies. It would be childish. Would half-past five do?

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Admirably! Admirably! And now, dear Mr. Worthing, I will not intrude any longer into a house of sorrow. I would merely beg you not to be too much bowed down by grief. What seem to us bitter trials are often blessings in disguise.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: This seems to me a blessing of an extremely obvious kind.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Uncle Jack! Oh, I am pleased to see you back. But what horrid clothes you have got on! Do go and change them.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Cecily!

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: My child! my child!

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: What is the matter, Uncle Jack? Do look happy! You look as if you had toothache, and I have got such a surprise for you. Who do you think is in the dining-room? Your brother!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Who?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Your brother Ernest. He arrived about half an hour ago.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: What nonsense! I haven’t got a brother.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh, don’t say that. However badly he may have behaved to you in the past he is still your brother. You couldn’t be so heartless as to disown him. I’ll tell him to come out. And you will shake hands with him, won’t you, Uncle Jack?

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: These are very joyful tidings.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: After we had all been resigned to his loss, his sudden return seems to me peculiarly distressing.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: My brother is in the dining-room? I don’t know what it all means. I think it is perfectly absurd.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Good heavens!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Brother John, I have come down from town to tell you that I am very sorry for all the trouble I have given you, and that I intend to lead a better life in the future.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Uncle Jack, you are not going to refuse your own brother’s hand?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Nothing will induce me to take his hand. I think his coming down here disgraceful. He knows perfectly well why.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Uncle Jack, do be nice. There is some good in every one. Ernest has just been telling me about his poor invalid friend Mr. Bunbury whom he goes to visit so often. And surely there must be much good in one who is kind to an invalid, and leaves the pleasures of London to sit by a bed of pain.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh! he has been talking about Bunbury, has he?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Yes, he has told me all about poor Mr. Bunbury, and his terrible state of health.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Bunbury! Well, I won’t have him talk to you about Bunbury or about anything else. It is enough to drive one perfectly frantic.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Of course I admit that the faults were all on my side. But I must say that I think that Brother John’s coldness to me is peculiarly painful. I expected a more enthusiastic welcome, especially considering it is the first time I have come here.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Uncle Jack, if you don’t shake hands with Ernest I will never forgive you.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Never forgive me?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Never, never, never!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, this is the last time I shall ever do it.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: It’s pleasant, is it not, to see so perfect a reconciliation? I think we might leave the two brothers together.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Cecily, you will come with us.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Certainly, Miss Prism. My little task of reconciliation is over.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: You have done a beautiful action to-day, dear child.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: We must not be premature in our judgments.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I feel very happy.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: You young scoundrel, Algy, you must get out of this place as soon as possible. I don’t allow any Bunburying here.

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: I have put Mr. Ernest’s things in the room next to yours, sir. I suppose that is all right?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: What?

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Mr. Ernest’s luggage, sir. I have unpacked it and put it in the room next to your own.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: His luggage?

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Yes, sir. Three portmanteaus, a dressing-case, two hat-boxes, and a large luncheon-basket.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I am afraid I can’t stay more than a week this time.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Merriman, order the dog-cart at once. Mr. Ernest has been suddenly called back to town.

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Yes, sir.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: What a fearful liar you are, Jack. I have not been called back to town at all.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Yes, you have.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I haven’t heard any one call me.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Your duty as a gentleman calls you back.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: My duty as a gentleman has never interfered with my pleasures in the smallest degree.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I can quite understand that.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, Cecily is a darling.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: You are not to talk of Miss Cardew like that. I don’t like it.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, I don’t like your clothes. You look perfectly ridiculous in them. Why on earth don’t you go up and change? It is perfectly childish to be in deep mourning for a man who is actually staying for a whole week with you in your house as a guest. I call it grotesque.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: You are certainly not staying with me for a whole week as a guest or anything else. You have got to leave . . . by the four-five train.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I certainly won’t leave you so long as you are in mourning. It would be most unfriendly. If I were in mourning you would stay with me, I suppose. I should think it very unkind if you didn’t.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, will you go if I change my clothes?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes, if you are not too long. I never saw anybody take so long to dress, and with such little result.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, at any rate, that is better than being always over-dressed as you are.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: If I am occasionally a little over-dressed, I make up for it by being always immensely over-educated.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Your vanity is ridiculous, your conduct an outrage, and your presence in my garden utterly absurd. However, you have got to catch the four-five, and I hope you will have a pleasant journey back to town. This Bunburying, as you call it, has not been a great success for you.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I think it has been a great success. I’m in love with Cecily, and that is everything. But I must see her before I go, and make arrangements for another Bunbury. Ah, there she is.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh, I merely came back to water the roses. I thought you were with Uncle Jack.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: He’s gone to order the dog-cart for me.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh, is he going to take you for a nice drive?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: He’s going to send me away.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Then have we got to part?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I am afraid so. It’s a very painful parting.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: It is always painful to part from people whom one has known for a very brief space of time. The absence of old friends one can endure with equanimity. But even a momentary separation from anyone to whom one has just been introduced is almost unbearable.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Thank you.

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: The dog-cart is at the door, sir.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: It can wait, Merriman for . . . five minutes.

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Yes, Miss.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I hope, Cecily, I shall not offend you if I state quite frankly and openly that you seem to me to be in every way the visible personification of absolute perfection.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I think your frankness does you great credit, Ernest. If you will allow me, I will copy your remarks into my diary.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Do you really keep a diary? I’d give anything to look at it. May I?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh no. You see, it is simply a very young girl’s record of her own thoughts and impressions, and consequently meant for publication. When it appears in volume form I hope you will order a copy. But pray, Ernest, don’t stop. I delight in taking down from dictation. I have reached ‘absolute perfection’. You can go on. I am quite ready for more.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Ahem! Ahem!

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh, don’t cough, Ernest. When one is dictating one should speak fluently and not cough. Besides, I don’t know how to spell a cough.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Cecily, ever since I first looked upon your wonderful and incomparable beauty, I have dared to love you wildly, passionately, devotedly, hopelessly.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I don’t think that you should tell me that you love me wildly, passionately, devotedly, hopelessly. Hopelessly doesn’t seem to make much sense, does it?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Cecily!

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: The dog-cart is waiting, sir.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Tell it to come round next week, at the same hour.

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Yes, sir.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Uncle Jack would be very much annoyed if he knew you were staying on till next week, at the same hour.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh, I don’t care about Jack. I don’t care for anybody in the whole world but you. I love you, Cecily. You will marry me, won’t you?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: You silly boy! Of course. Why, we have been engaged for the last three months.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: For the last three months?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Yes, it will be exactly three months on Thursday.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: But how did we become engaged?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Well, ever since dear Uncle Jack first confessed to us that he had a younger brother who was very wicked and bad, you of course have formed the chief topic of conversation between myself and Miss Prism. And of course a man who is much talked about is always very attractive. One feels there must be something in him, after all. I daresay it was foolish of me, but I fell in love with you, Ernest.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Darling! And when was the engagement actually settled?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: On the 14th of February last. Worn out by your entire ignorance of my existence, I determined to end the matter one way or the other, and after a long struggle with myself I accepted you under this dear old tree here. The next day I bought this little ring in your name, and this is the little bangle with the true lover’s knot I promised you always to wear.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Did I give you this? It’s very pretty, isn’t it?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Yes, you’ve wonderfully good taste, Ernest. It’s the excuse I’ve always given for your leading such a bad life. And this is the box in which I keep all your dear letters.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: My letters! But, my own sweet Cecily, I have never written you any letters.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: You need hardly remind me of that, Ernest. I remember only too well that I was forced to write your letters for you. I wrote always three times a week, and sometimes oftener.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh, do let me read them, Cecily?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh, I couldn’t possibly. They would make you far too conceited. The three you wrote me after I had broken off the engagement are so beautiful, and so badly spelled, that even now I can hardly read them without crying a little.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: But was our engagement ever broken off?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Of course it was. On the 22nd of last March. You can see the entry if you like. ‘To-day I broke off my engagement with Ernest. I feel it is better to do so. The weather still continues charming.’

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: But why on earth did you break it off? What had I done? I had done nothing at all. Cecily, I am very much hurt indeed to hear you broke it off. Particularly when the weather was so charming.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: It would hardly have been a really serious engagement if it hadn’t been broken off at least once. But I forgave you before the week was out.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: What a perfect angel you are, Cecily.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: You dear romantic boy. I hope your hair curls naturally, does it?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes, darling, with a little help from others.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I am so glad.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: You’ll never break off our engagement again, Cecily?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I don’t think I could break it off now that I have actually met you. Besides, of course, there is the question of your name.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes, of course.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: You must not laugh at me, darling, but it had always been a girlish dream of mine to love some one whose name was Ernest. There is something in that name that seems to inspire absolute confidence. I pity any poor married woman whose husband is not called Ernest.
