speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: But, my dear child, do you mean to say you could not love me if I had some other name?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: But what name?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh, any name you like—Algernon—for instance . . .

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: But I don’t like the name of Algernon.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, my own dear, sweet, loving little darling, I really can’t see why you should object to the name of Algernon. It is not at all a bad name. In fact, it is rather an aristocratic name. Half of the chaps who get into the Bankruptcy Court are called Algernon. But seriously, Cecily . . .. . if my name was Algy, couldn’t you love me?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I might respect you, Ernest, I might admire your character, but I fear that I should not be able to give you my undivided attention.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Ahem! Cecily! Your Rector here is, I suppose, thoroughly experienced in the practice of all the rites and ceremonials of the Church?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh, yes. Dr. Chasuble is a most learned man. He has never written a single book, so you can imagine how much he knows.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I must see him at once on a most important christening—I mean on most important business.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I shan’t be away more than half an hour.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Considering that we have been engaged since February the 14th, and that I only met you to-day for the first time, I think it is rather hard that you should leave me for so long a period as half an hour. Couldn’t you make it twenty minutes?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I’ll be back in no time.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: What an impetuous boy he is! I like his hair so much. I must enter his proposal in my diary.

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: A Miss Fairfax has just called to see Mr. Worthing. On very important business, Miss Fairfax states.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Isn’t Mr. Worthing in his library?

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Mr. Worthing went over in the direction of the Rectory some time ago.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Pray ask the lady to come out here; Mr. Worthing is sure to be back soon. And you can bring tea.

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Yes, Miss.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Miss Fairfax! I suppose one of the many good elderly women who are associated with Uncle Jack in some of his philanthropic work in London. I don’t quite like women who are interested in philanthropic work. I think it is so forward of them.

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Miss Fairfax.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Pray let me introduce myself to you. My name is Cecily Cardew.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Cecily Cardew? What a very sweet name! Something tells me that we are going to be great friends. I like you already more than I can say. My first impressions of people are never wrong.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: How nice of you to like me so much after we have known each other such a comparatively short time. Pray sit down.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I may call you Cecily, may I not?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: With pleasure!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: And you will always call me Gwendolen, won’t you?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: If you wish.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Then that is all quite settled, is it not?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I hope so.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Perhaps this might be a favourable opportunity for my mentioning who I am. My father is Lord Bracknell. You have never heard of papa, I suppose?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I don’t think so.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Outside the family circle, papa, I am glad to say, is entirely unknown. I think that is quite as it should be. The home seems to me to be the proper sphere for the man. And certainly once a man begins to neglect his domestic duties he becomes painfully effeminate, does he not? And I don’t like that. It makes men so very attractive. Cecily, mamma, whose views on education are remarkably strict, has brought me up to be extremely short-sighted; it is part of her system; so do you mind my looking at you through my glasses?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh! not at all, Gwendolen. I am very fond of being looked at.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: You are here on a short visit, I suppose.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh no! I live here.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Really? Your mother, no doubt, or some female relative of advanced years, resides here also?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh no! I have no mother, nor, in fact, any relations.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Indeed?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: My dear guardian, with the assistance of Miss Prism, has the arduous task of looking after me.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Your guardian?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Yes, I am Mr. Worthing’s ward.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Oh! It is strange he never mentioned to me that he had a ward. How secretive of him! He grows more interesting hourly. I am not sure, however, that the news inspires me with feelings of unmixed delight. I am very fond of you, Cecily; I have liked you ever since I met you! But I am bound to state that now that I know that you are Mr. Worthing’s ward, I cannot help expressing a wish you were—well, just a little older than you seem to be—and not quite so very alluring in appearance. In fact, if I may speak candidly—

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Pray do! I think that whenever one has anything unpleasant to say, one should always be quite candid.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Well, to speak with perfect candour, Cecily, I wish that you were fully forty-two, and more than usually plain for your age. Ernest has a strong upright nature. He is the very soul of truth and honour. Disloyalty would be as impossible to him as deception. But even men of the noblest possible moral character are extremely susceptible to the influence of the physical charms of others. Modern, no less than Ancient History, supplies us with many most painful examples of what I refer to. If it were not so, indeed, History would be quite unreadable.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I beg your pardon, Gwendolen, did you say Ernest?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh, but it is not Mr. Ernest Worthing who is my guardian. It is his brother—his elder brother.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Ernest never mentioned to me that he had a brother.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I am sorry to say they have not been on good terms for a long time.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Ah! that accounts for it. And now that I think of it I have never heard any man mention his brother. The subject seems distasteful to most men. Cecily, you have lifted a load from my mind. I was growing almost anxious. It would have been terrible if any cloud had come across a friendship like ours, would it not? Of course you are quite, quite sure that it is not Mr. Ernest Worthing who is your guardian?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Quite sure. In fact, I am going to be his.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I beg your pardon?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Dearest Gwendolen, there is no reason why I should make a secret of it to you. Our little county newspaper is sure to chronicle the fact next week. Mr. Ernest Worthing and I are engaged to be married.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: My darling Cecily, I think there must be some slight error. Mr. Ernest Worthing is engaged to me. The announcement will appear in the Morning Post on Saturday at the latest.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I am afraid you must be under some misconception. Ernest proposed to me exactly ten minutes ago.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: It is certainly very curious, for he asked me to be his wife yesterday afternoon at 5.30. If you would care to verify the incident, pray do so. I never travel without my diary. One should always have something sensational to read in the train. I am so sorry, dear Cecily, if it is any disappointment to you, but I am afraid I have the prior claim.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: It would distress me more than I can tell you, dear Gwendolen, if it caused you any mental or physical anguish, but I feel bound to point out that since Ernest proposed to you he clearly has changed his mind.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: If the poor fellow has been entrapped into any foolish promise I shall consider it my duty to rescue him at once, and with a firm hand.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Whatever unfortunate entanglement my dear boy may have got into, I will never reproach him with it after we are married.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Do you allude to me, Miss Cardew, as an entanglement? You are presumptuous. On an occasion of this kind it becomes more than a moral duty to speak one’s mind. It becomes a pleasure.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Do you suggest, Miss Fairfax, that I entrapped Ernest into an engagement? How dare you? This is no time for wearing the shallow mask of manners. When I see a spade I call it a spade.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I am glad to say that I have never seen a spade. It is obvious that our social spheres have been widely different.

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Shall I lay tea here as usual, Miss?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Yes, as usual.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Are there many interesting walks in the vicinity, Miss Cardew?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh! yes! a great many. From the top of one of the hills quite close one can see five counties.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Five counties! I don’t think I should like that; I hate crowds.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I suppose that is why you live in town?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Quite a well-kept garden this is, Miss Cardew.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: So glad you like it, Miss Fairfax.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I had no idea there were any flowers in the country.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh, flowers are as common here, Miss Fairfax, as people are in London.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Personally I cannot understand how anybody manages to exist in the country, if anybody who is anybody does. The country always bores me to death.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Ah! This is what the newspapers call agricultural depression, is it not? I believe the aristocracy are suffering very much from it just at present. It is almost an epidemic amongst them, I have been told. May I offer you some tea, Miss Fairfax?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Thank you. Detestable girl! But I require tea!

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Sugar?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: No, thank you. Sugar is not fashionable any more.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Cake or bread and butter?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Bread and butter, please. Cake is rarely seen at the best houses nowadays.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Hand that to Miss Fairfax.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: You have filled my tea with lumps of sugar, and though I asked most distinctly for bread and butter, you have given me cake. I am known for the gentleness of my disposition, and the extraordinary sweetness of my nature, but I warn you, Miss Cardew, you may go too far.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: To save my poor, innocent, trusting boy from the machinations of any other girl there are no lengths to which I would not go.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: From the moment I saw you I distrusted you. I felt that you were false and deceitful. I am never deceived in such matters. My first impressions of people are invariably right.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: It seems to me, Miss Fairfax, that I am trespassing on your valuable time. No doubt you have many other calls of a similar character to make in the neighbourhood.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Ernest! My own Ernest!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Gwendolen! Darling!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: A moment! May I ask if you are engaged to be married to this young lady?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: To dear little Cecily! Of course not! What could have put such an idea into your pretty little head?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Thank you. You may!

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I knew there must be some misunderstanding, Miss Fairfax. The gentleman whose arm is at present round your waist is my guardian, Mr. John Worthing.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I beg your pardon?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: This is Uncle Jack.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Jack! Oh!

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Here is Ernest.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: My own love!

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: A moment, Ernest! May I ask you—are you engaged to be married to this young lady?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: To what young lady? Good heavens! Gwendolen!

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Yes! to good heavens, Gwendolen, I mean to Gwendolen.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Of course not! What could have put such an idea into your pretty little head?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Thank you. You may.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I felt there was some slight error, Miss Cardew. The gentleman who is now embracing you is my cousin, Mr. Algernon Moncrieff.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Algernon Moncrieff! Oh!

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Are you called Algernon?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I cannot deny it.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Oh!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Is your name really John?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I could deny it if I liked. I could deny anything if I liked. But my name certainly is John. It has been John for years.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: A gross deception has been practised on both of us.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: My poor wounded Cecily!

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: My sweet wronged Gwendolen!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: You will call me sister, will you not?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: There is just one question I would like to be allowed to ask my guardian.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: An admirable idea! Mr. Worthing, there is just one question I would like to be permitted to put to you. Where is your brother Ernest? We are both engaged to be married to your brother Ernest, so it is a matter of some importance to us to know where your brother Ernest is at present.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Gwendolen—Cecily—it is very painful for me to be forced to speak the truth. It is the first time in my life that I have ever been reduced to such a painful position, and I am really quite inexperienced in doing anything of the kind. However, I will tell you quite frankly that I have no brother Ernest. I have no brother at all. I never had a brother in my life, and I certainly have not the smallest intention of ever having one in the future.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: No brother at all?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: None!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Had you never a brother of any kind?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Never. Not even of any kind.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I am afraid it is quite clear, Cecily, that neither of us is engaged to be married to any one.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: It is not a very pleasant position for a young girl suddenly to find herself in. Is it?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Let us go into the house. They will hardly venture to come after us there.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: No, men are so cowardly, aren’t they?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: This ghastly state of things is what you call Bunburying, I suppose?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes, and a perfectly wonderful Bunbury it is. The most wonderful Bunbury I have ever had in my life.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, you’ve no right whatsoever to Bunbury here.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: That is absurd. One has a right to Bunbury anywhere one chooses. Every serious Bunburyist knows that.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Serious Bunburyist! Good heavens!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, one must be serious about something, if one wants to have any amusement in life. I happen to be serious about Bunburying. What on earth you are serious about I haven’t got the remotest idea. About everything, I should fancy. You have such an absolutely trivial nature.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, the only small satisfaction I have in the whole of this wretched business is that your friend Bunbury is quite exploded. You won’t be able to run down to the country quite so often as you used to do, dear Algy. And a very good thing too.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Your brother is a little off colour, isn’t he, dear Jack? You won’t be able to disappear to London quite so frequently as your wicked custom was. And not a bad thing either.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: As for your conduct towards Miss Cardew, I must say that your taking in a sweet, simple, innocent girl like that is quite inexcusable. To say nothing of the fact that she is my ward.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I can see no possible defence at all for your deceiving a brilliant, clever, thoroughly experienced young lady like Miss Fairfax. To say nothing of the fact that she is my cousin.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I wanted to be engaged to Gwendolen, that is all. I love her.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, I simply wanted to be engaged to Cecily. I adore her.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: There is certainly no chance of your marrying Miss Cardew.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I don’t think there is much likelihood, Jack, of you and Miss Fairfax being united.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, that is no business of yours.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: If it was my business, I wouldn’t talk about it. It is very vulgar to talk about one’s business. Only people like stock-brokers do that, and then merely at dinner parties.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: How can you sit there, calmly eating muffins when we are in this horrible trouble, I can’t make out. You seem to me to be perfectly heartless.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, I can’t eat muffins in an agitated manner. The butter would probably get on my cuffs. One should always eat muffins quite calmly. It is the only way to eat them.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I say it’s perfectly heartless your eating muffins at all, under the circumstances.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: When I am in trouble, eating is the only thing that consoles me. Indeed, when I am in really great trouble, as any one who knows me intimately will tell you, I refuse everything except food and drink. At the present moment I am eating muffins because I am unhappy. Besides, I am particularly fond of muffins.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Well, that is no reason why you should eat them all in that greedy way.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I wish you would have tea-cake instead. I don’t like tea-cake.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Good heavens! I suppose a man may eat his own muffins in his own garden.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: But you have just said it was perfectly heartless to eat muffins.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I said it was perfectly heartless of you, under the circumstances. That is a very different thing.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: That may be. But the muffins are the same.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Algy, I wish to goodness you would go.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: You can’t possibly ask me to go without having some dinner. It’s absurd. I never go without my dinner. No one ever does, except vegetarians and people like that. Besides I have just made arrangements with Dr. Chasuble to be christened at a quarter to six under the name of Ernest.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: My dear fellow, the sooner you give up that nonsense the better. I made arrangements this morning with Dr. Chasuble to be christened myself at 5.30, and I naturally will take the name of Ernest. Gwendolen would wish it. We can’t both be christened Ernest. It’s absurd. Besides, I have a perfect right to be christened if I like. There is no evidence at all that I have ever been christened by anybody. I should think it extremely probable I never was, and so does Dr. Chasuble. It is entirely different in your case. You have been christened already.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes, but I have not been christened for years.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Yes, but you have been christened. That is the important thing.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Quite so. So I know my constitution can stand it. If you are not quite sure about your ever having been christened, I must say I think it rather dangerous your venturing on it now. It might make you very unwell. You can hardly have forgotten that some one very closely connected with you was very nearly carried off this week in Paris by a severe chill.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Yes, but you said yourself that a severe chill was not hereditary.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: It usen’t to be, I know—but I daresay it is now. Science is always making wonderful improvements in things.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh, that is nonsense; you are always talking nonsense.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Jack, you are at the muffins again! I wish you wouldn’t. There are only two left. I told you I was particularly fond of muffins.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: But I hate tea-cake.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Why on earth then do you allow tea-cake to be served up for your guests? What ideas you have of hospitality!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Algernon! I have already told you to go. I don’t want you here. Why don’t you go!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I haven’t quite finished my tea yet! and there is still one muffin left.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: The fact that they did not follow us at once into the house, as any one else would have done, seems to me to show that they have some sense of shame left.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: They have been eating muffins. That looks like repentance.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: They don’t seem to notice us at all. Couldn’t you cough?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: But I haven’t got a cough.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: They’re looking at us. What effrontery!

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: They’re approaching. That’s very forward of them.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Let us preserve a dignified silence.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Certainly. It’s the only thing to do now.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: This dignified silence seems to produce an unpleasant effect.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: A most distasteful one.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: But we will not be the first to speak.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Certainly not.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Mr. Worthing, I have something very particular to ask you. Much depends on your reply.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Gwendolen, your common sense is invaluable. Mr. Moncrieff, kindly answer me the following question. Why did you pretend to be my guardian’s brother?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: In order that I might have an opportunity of meeting you.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: That certainly seems a satisfactory explanation, does it not?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Yes, dear, if you can believe him.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I don’t. But that does not affect the wonderful beauty of his answer.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: True. In matters of grave importance, style, not sincerity is the vital thing. Mr. Worthing, what explanation can you offer to me for pretending to have a brother? Was it in order that you might have an opportunity of coming up to town to see me as often as possible?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Can you doubt it, Miss Fairfax?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I have the gravest doubts upon the subject. But I intend to crush them. This is not the moment for German scepticism. Their explanations appear to be quite satisfactory, especially Mr. Worthing’s. That seems to me to have the stamp of truth upon it.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I am more than content with what Mr. Moncrieff said. His voice alone inspires one with absolute credulity.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Then you think we should forgive them?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Yes. I mean no.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: True! I had forgotten. There are principles at stake that one cannot surrender. Which of us should tell them? The task is not a pleasant one.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Could we not both speak at the same time?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: An excellent idea! I nearly always speak at the same time as other people. Will you take the time from me?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Certainly.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN and CECILY
speeches.text: Your Christian names are still an insuperable barrier. That is all!

speeches.speaker: JACK and ALGERNON
speeches.text: Our Christian names! Is that all? But we are going to be christened this afternoon.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: For my sake you are prepared to do this terrible thing?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I am.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: To please me you are ready to face this fearful ordeal?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I am!

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: How absurd to talk of the equality of the sexes! Where questions of self-sacrifice are concerned, men are infinitely beyond us.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: We are.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: They have moments of physical courage of which we women know absolutely nothing.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Darling!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Darling!

speeches.speaker: MERRIMAN
speeches.text: Ahem! Ahem! Lady Bracknell!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Good heavens!

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Gwendolen! What does this mean?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Merely that I am engaged to be married to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Come here. Sit down. Sit down immediately. Hesitation of any kind is a sign of mental decay in the young, of physical weakness in the old. Apprised, sir, of my daughter’s sudden flight by her trusty maid, whose confidence I purchased by means of a small coin, I followed her at once by a luggage train. Her unhappy father is, I am glad to say, under the impression that she is attending a more than usually lengthy lecture by the University Extension Scheme on the Influence of a permanent income on Thought. I do not propose to undeceive him. Indeed I have never undeceived him on any question. I would consider it wrong. But of course, you will clearly understand that all communication between yourself and my daughter must cease immediately from this moment. On this point, as indeed on all points, I am firm.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I am engaged to be married to Gwendolen, Lady Bracknell!

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: You are nothing of the kind, sir. And now, as regards Algernon! . . . Algernon!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes, Aunt Augusta.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: May I ask if it is in this house that your invalid friend Mr. Bunbury resides?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh! No! Bunbury doesn’t live here. Bunbury is somewhere else at present. In fact, Bunbury is dead.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Dead! When did Mr. Bunbury die? His death must have been extremely sudden.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Oh! I killed Bunbury this afternoon. I mean poor Bunbury died this afternoon.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: What did he die of?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Bunbury? Oh, he was quite exploded.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Exploded! Was he the victim of a revolutionary outrage? I was not aware that Mr. Bunbury was interested in social legislation. If so, he is well punished for his morbidity.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: My dear Aunt Augusta, I mean he was found out! The doctors found out that Bunbury could not live, that is what I mean—so Bunbury died.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: He seems to have had great confidence in the opinion of his physicians. I am glad, however, that he made up his mind at the last to some definite course of action, and acted under proper medical advice. And now that we have finally got rid of this Mr. Bunbury, may I ask, Mr. Worthing, who is that young person whose hand my nephew Algernon is now holding in what seems to me a peculiarly unnecessary manner?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: That lady is Miss Cecily Cardew, my ward.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: I am engaged to be married to Cecily, Aunt Augusta.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I beg your pardon?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Mr. Moncrieff and I are engaged to be married, Lady Bracknell.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I do not know whether there is anything peculiarly exciting in the air of this particular part of Hertfordshire, but the number of engagements that go on seems to me considerably above the proper average that statistics have laid down for our guidance. I think some preliminary inquiry on my part would not be out of place. Mr. Worthing, is Miss Cardew at all connected with any of the larger railway stations in London? I merely desire information. Until yesterday I had no idea that there were any families or persons whose origin was a Terminus.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Miss Cardew is the grand-daughter of the late Mr. Thomas Cardew of 149 Belgrave Square, S.W.; Gervase Park, Dorking, Surrey; and the Sporran, Fifeshire, N.B.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: That sounds not unsatisfactory. Three addresses always inspire confidence, even in tradesmen. But what proof have I of their authenticity?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I have carefully preserved the Court Guides of the period. They are open to your inspection, Lady Bracknell.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I have known strange errors in that publication.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Miss Cardew’s family solicitors are Messrs. Markby, Markby, and Markby.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Markby, Markby, and Markby? A firm of the very highest position in their profession. Indeed I am told that one of the Mr. Markby’s is occasionally to be seen at dinner parties. So far I am satisfied.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: How extremely kind of you, Lady Bracknell! I have also in my possession, you will be pleased to hear, certificates of Miss Cardew’s birth, baptism, whooping cough, registration, vaccination, confirmation, and the measles; both the German and the English variety.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Ah! A life crowded with incident, I see; though perhaps somewhat too exciting for a young girl. I am not myself in favour of premature experiences. Gwendolen! the time approaches for our departure. We have not a moment to lose. As a matter of form, Mr. Worthing, I had better ask you if Miss Cardew has any little fortune?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Oh! about a hundred and thirty thousand pounds in the Funds. That is all. Goodbye, Lady Bracknell. So pleased to have seen you.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: A moment, Mr. Worthing. A hundred and thirty thousand pounds! And in the Funds! Miss Cardew seems to me a most attractive young lady, now that I look at her. Few girls of the present day have any really solid qualities, any of the qualities that last, and improve with time. We live, I regret to say, in an age of surfaces. Come over here, dear. Pretty child! your dress is sadly simple, and your hair seems almost as Nature might have left it. But we can soon alter all that. A thoroughly experienced French maid produces a really marvellous result in a very brief space of time. I remember recommending one to young Lady Lancing, and after three months her own husband did not know her.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: And after six months nobody knew her.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Kindly turn round, sweet child. No, the side view is what I want. Yes, quite as I expected. There are distinct social possibilities in your profile. The two weak points in our age are its want of principle and its want of profile. The chin a little higher, dear. Style largely depends on the way the chin is worn. They are worn very high, just at present. Algernon!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Yes, Aunt Augusta!

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: There are distinct social possibilities in Miss Cardew’s profile.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Cecily is the sweetest, dearest, prettiest girl in the whole world. And I don’t care twopence about social possibilities.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Never speak disrespectfully of Society, Algernon. Only people who can’t get into it do that. Dear child, of course you know that Algernon has nothing but his debts to depend upon. But I do not approve of mercenary marriages. When I married Lord Bracknell I had no fortune of any kind. But I never dreamed for a moment of allowing that to stand in my way. Well, I suppose I must give my consent.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Thank you, Aunt Augusta.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Cecily, you may kiss me!

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: You may also address me as Aunt Augusta for the future.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Thank you, Aunt Augusta.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: The marriage, I think, had better take place quite soon.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Thank you, Aunt Augusta.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Thank you, Aunt Augusta.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: To speak frankly, I am not in favour of long engagements. They give people the opportunity of finding out each other’s character before marriage, which I think is never advisable.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I beg your pardon for interrupting you, Lady Bracknell, but this engagement is quite out of the question. I am Miss Cardew’s guardian, and she cannot marry without my consent until she comes of age. That consent I absolutely decline to give.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Upon what grounds may I ask? Algernon is an extremely, I may almost say an ostentatiously, eligible young man. He has nothing, but he looks everything. What more can one desire?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: It pains me very much to have to speak frankly to you, Lady Bracknell, about your nephew, but the fact is that I do not approve at all of his moral character. I suspect him of being untruthful.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Untruthful! My nephew Algernon? Impossible! He is an Oxonian.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I fear there can be no possible doubt about the matter. This afternoon during my temporary absence in London on an important question of romance, he obtained admission to my house by means of the false pretence of being my brother. Under an assumed name he drank, I’ve just been informed by my butler, an entire pint bottle of my Perrier-Jouet, Brut, ’89; wine I was specially reserving for myself. Continuing his disgraceful deception, he succeeded in the course of the afternoon in alienating the affections of my only ward. He subsequently stayed to tea, and devoured every single muffin. And what makes his conduct all the more heartless is, that he was perfectly well aware from the first that I have no brother, that I never had a brother, and that I don’t intend to have a brother, not even of any kind. I distinctly told him so myself yesterday afternoon.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Ahem! Mr. Worthing, after careful consideration I have decided entirely to overlook my nephew’s conduct to you.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: That is very generous of you, Lady Bracknell. My own decision, however, is unalterable. I decline to give my consent.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Come here, sweet child. How old are you, dear?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Well, I am really only eighteen, but I always admit to twenty when I go to evening parties.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: You are perfectly right in making some slight alteration. Indeed, no woman should ever be quite accurate about her age. It looks so calculating . . . Eighteen, but admitting to twenty at evening parties. Well, it will not be very long before you are of age and free from the restraints of tutelage. So I don’t think your guardian’s consent is, after all, a matter of any importance.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Pray excuse me, Lady Bracknell, for interrupting you again, but it is only fair to tell you that according to the terms of her grandfather’s will Miss Cardew does not come legally of age till she is thirty-five.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: That does not seem to me to be a grave objection. Thirty-five is a very attractive age. London society is full of women of the very highest birth who have, of their own free choice, remained thirty-five for years. Lady Dumbleton is an instance in point. To my own knowledge she has been thirty-five ever since she arrived at the age of forty, which was many years ago now. I see no reason why our dear Cecily should not be even still more attractive at the age you mention than she is at present. There will be a large accumulation of property.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Algy, could you wait for me till I was thirty-five?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Of course I could, Cecily. You know I could.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Yes, I felt it instinctively, but I couldn’t wait all that time. I hate waiting even five minutes for anybody. It always makes me rather cross. I am not punctual myself, I know, but I do like punctuality in others, and waiting, even to be married, is quite out of the question.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Then what is to be done, Cecily?

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: I don’t know, Mr. Moncrieff.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: My dear Mr. Worthing, as Miss Cardew states positively that she cannot wait till she is thirty-five—a remark which I am bound to say seems to me to show a somewhat impatient nature—I would beg of you to reconsider your decision.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: But my dear Lady Bracknell, the matter is entirely in your own hands. The moment you consent to my marriage with Gwendolen, I will most gladly allow your nephew to form an alliance with my ward.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: You must be quite aware that what you propose is out of the question.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Then a passionate celibacy is all that any of us can look forward to.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: That is not the destiny I propose for Gwendolen. Algernon, of course, can choose for himself. Come, dear, we have already missed five, if not six, trains. To miss any more might expose us to comment on the platform.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Everything is quite ready for the christenings.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: The christenings, sir! Is not that somewhat premature?

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Both these gentlemen have expressed a desire for immediate baptism.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: At their age? The idea is grotesque and irreligious! Algernon, I forbid you to be baptized. I will not hear of such excesses. Lord Bracknell would be highly displeased if he learned that that was the way in which you wasted your time and money.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Am I to understand then that there are to be no christenings at all this afternoon?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I don’t think that, as things are now, it would be of much practical value to either of us, Dr. Chasuble.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: I am grieved to hear such sentiments from you, Mr. Worthing. They savour of the heretical views of the Anabaptists, views that I have completely refuted in four of my unpublished sermons. However, as your present mood seems to be one peculiarly secular, I will return to the church at once. Indeed, I have just been informed by the pew-opener that for the last hour and a half Miss Prism has been waiting for me in the vestry.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Miss Prism! Did I hear you mention a Miss Prism?

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Yes, Lady Bracknell. I am on my way to join her.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Pray allow me to detain you for a moment. This matter may prove to be one of vital importance to Lord Bracknell and myself. Is this Miss Prism a female of repellent aspect, remotely connected with education?

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: She is the most cultivated of ladies, and the very picture of respectability.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: It is obviously the same person. May I ask what position she holds in your household?

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: I am a celibate, madam.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Miss Prism, Lady Bracknell, has been for the last three years Miss Cardew’s esteemed governess and valued companion.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: In spite of what I hear of her, I must see her at once. Let her be sent for.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: She approaches; she is nigh.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: I was told you expected me in the vestry, dear Canon. I have been waiting for you there for an hour and three-quarters.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Prism! Come here, Prism! Prism! Where is that baby? Twenty-eight years ago, Prism, you left Lord Bracknell’s house, Number 104, Upper Grosvenor Street, in charge of a perambulator that contained a baby of the male sex. You never returned. A few weeks later, through the elaborate investigations of the Metropolitan police, the perambulator was discovered at midnight, standing by itself in a remote corner of Bayswater. It contained the manuscript of a three-volume novel of more than usually revolting sentimentality. But the baby was not there! Prism! Where is that baby?

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Lady Bracknell, I admit with shame that I do not know. I only wish I did. The plain facts of the case are these. On the morning of the day you mention, a day that is for ever branded on my memory, I prepared as usual to take the baby out in its perambulator. I had also with me a somewhat old, but capacious hand-bag in which I had intended to place the manuscript of a work of fiction that I had written during my few unoccupied hours. In a moment of mental abstraction, for which I never can forgive myself, I deposited the manuscript in the basinette, and placed the baby in the hand-bag.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: But where did you deposit the hand-bag?

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Do not ask me, Mr. Worthing.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Miss Prism, this is a matter of no small importance to me. I insist on knowing where you deposited the hand-bag that contained that infant.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: I left it in the cloak-room of one of the larger railway stations in London.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: What railway station?

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Victoria. The Brighton line.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: I must retire to my room for a moment. Gwendolen, wait here for me.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: If you are not too long, I will wait here for you all my life.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: What do you think this means, Lady Bracknell?

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I dare not even suspect, Dr. Chasuble. I need hardly tell you that in families of high position strange coincidences are not supposed to occur. They are hardly considered the thing.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: Uncle Jack seems strangely agitated.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Your guardian has a very emotional nature.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: This noise is extremely unpleasant. It sounds as if he was having an argument. I dislike arguments of any kind. They are always vulgar, and often convincing.

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: It has stopped now.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I wish he would arrive at some conclusion.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: This suspense is terrible. I hope it will last.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Is this the hand-bag, Miss Prism? Examine it carefully before you speak. The happiness of more than one life depends on your answer.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: It seems to be mine. Yes, here is the injury it received through the upsetting of a Gower Street omnibus in younger and happier days. Here is the stain on the lining caused by the explosion of a temperance beverage, an incident that occurred at Leamington. And here, on the lock, are my initials. I had forgotten that in an extravagant mood I had had them placed there. The bag is undoubtedly mine. I am delighted to have it so unexpectedly restored to me. It has been a great inconvenience being without it all these years.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Miss Prism, more is restored to you than this hand-bag. I was the baby you placed in it.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: You?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Yes . . . mother!

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Mr. Worthing! I am unmarried!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Unmarried! I do not deny that is a serious blow. But after all, who has the right to cast a stone against one who has suffered? Cannot repentance wipe out an act of folly? Why should there be one law for men, and another for women? Mother, I forgive you.

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Mr. Worthing, there is some error. There is the lady who can tell you who you really are.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Lady Bracknell, I hate to seem inquisitive, but would you kindly inform me who I am?

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I am afraid that the news I have to give you will not altogether please you. You are the son of my poor sister, Mrs. Moncrieff, and consequently Algernon’s elder brother.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Algy’s elder brother! Then I have a brother after all. I knew I had a brother! I always said I had a brother! Cecily,—how could you have ever doubted that I had a brother? Dr. Chasuble, my unfortunate brother. Miss Prism, my unfortunate brother. Gwendolen, my unfortunate brother. Algy, you young scoundrel, you will have to treat me with more respect in the future. You have never behaved to me like a brother in all your life.

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Well, not till to-day, old boy, I admit. I did my best, however, though I was out of practice.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: My own! But what own are you? What is your Christian name, now that you have become some one else?

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Good heavens! . . . I had quite forgotten that point. Your decision on the subject of my name is irrevocable, I suppose?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I never change, except in my affections.

speeches.speaker: CECILY
speeches.text: What a noble nature you have, Gwendolen!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Then the question had better be cleared up at once. Aunt Augusta, a moment. At the time when Miss Prism left me in the hand-bag, had I been christened already?

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Every luxury that money could buy, including christening, had been lavished on you by your fond and doting parents.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Then I was christened! That is settled. Now, what name was I given? Let me know the worst.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Being the eldest son you were naturally christened after your father.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Yes, but what was my father’s Christian name?

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: I cannot at the present moment recall what the General’s Christian name was. But I have no doubt he had one. He was eccentric, I admit. But only in later years. And that was the result of the Indian climate, and marriage, and indigestion, and other things of that kind.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Algy! Can’t you recollect what our father’s Christian name was?

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: My dear boy, we were never even on speaking terms. He died before I was a year old.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: His name would appear in the Army Lists of the period, I suppose, Aunt Augusta?

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: The General was essentially a man of peace, except in his domestic life. But I have no doubt his name would appear in any military directory.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: The Army Lists of the last forty years are here. These delightful records should have been my constant study. M. Generals . . . Mallam, Maxbohm, Magley, what ghastly names they have—Markby, Migsby, Mobbs, Moncrieff! Lieutenant 1840, Captain, Lieutenant-Colonel, Colonel, General 1869, Christian names, Ernest John. I always told you, Gwendolen, my name was Ernest, didn’t I? Well, it is Ernest after all. I mean it naturally is Ernest.

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: Yes, I remember now that the General was called Ernest, I knew I had some particular reason for disliking the name.

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: Ernest! My own Ernest! I felt from the first that you could have no other name!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Gwendolen, it is a terrible thing for a man to find out suddenly that all his life he has been speaking nothing but the truth. Can you forgive me?

speeches.speaker: GWENDOLEN
speeches.text: I can. For I feel that you are sure to change.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: My own one!

speeches.speaker: CHASUBLE
speeches.text: Lætitia!

speeches.speaker: MISS PRISM
speeches.text: Frederick! At last!

speeches.speaker: ALGERNON
speeches.text: Cecily! At last!

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: Gwendolen! At last!

speeches.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
speeches.text: My nephew, you seem to be displaying signs of triviality.

speeches.speaker: JACK
speeches.text: On the contrary, Aunt Augusta, I’ve now realised for the first time in my life the vital Importance of Being Earnest.
